theater: 解州神稷山寨與陝州前線

battle.name: 邵興抗金起義
battle.theater: 解州神稷山寨與陝州前線
battle.brief: 靖康二年正月，汴京陷落，北宋覆亡，河東郡縣望風而降。解州安邑人邵興散財結眾，於解州西北神稷山築寨，據鹽池、斷糧道，與金軍相持四五年。紹興元年陝州失守，他突圍南下，改名邵隆，退守商州十餘年。卡面的維京長斧未曾在河東出現，但它窄面單刃、以重量取勢的邏輯，正是義軍以柴斧、朴刀在山道設伏時所倚仗者。

kit.name: 維京長斧
kit.history: 刃很長，斧面窄。北歐的船隊帶著它，也帶著它上岸。

countries: 交戰的兩面，一邊是剛滅掉北宋的金朝在河東的統治機器：女真猛安、謀克為骨幹，漢人與契丹降軍為輔，於河東路、河南路分置統軍司與州縣駐軍，另以討捕的名目臨時徵發河北、山東兵馬；金廷倚河東的產鹽區為重要財源，解州鹽池的鹽利幾乎等於一筆常設軍費，所以任何占住解州的武裝都直接觸動金朝財政。另一邊是邵興在解州西北神稷山拉起來的鄉里義軍：起手是安邑、聞喜一帶的鹽丁、農戶、獵戶與散卒，多是失去廩食的移民和不能隨官軍南退的北方百姓，人數由數十、數百漸聚至數千、數萬。義軍並無常備建制，只以邵興為首領，設偏將、隊帥分領各部，糧秣靠寨屯與取自敵方的物資，對百姓則約束甚嚴，據說下令不許劫掠、擄掠，士卒有侵擾鄉里者即行誅除，以免金人得以為口實。金人視之為流寇，郡縣視之為更大的流寇，兩面都不把它當軍伍看待。同期北方還有曹成的八字軍在山東、張榮的紅巾軍在泰山、馬擴在河北五馬山寨各立旗號，彼此以響應相勵，卻沒有統一指揮，也沒有聯合行動的機制，消息靠商旅、驛騎與逃戶零星傳遞。
countriesEn: Two sides stood against each other. On one side stood the Jin state’s war machine in Hedong, which had only just destroyed the Northern Song: Jurchen meng'an and mouke tribal regiments formed the backbone, with Han and Khitan surrendered troops as auxiliaries, distributed across the Hedong and Henan circuits as commanderies and garrison cities, and with troops hastily levied from Hebei and Shandong under the label of suppression expeditions. The Jin court depended heavily on the salt-producing districts of Hedong; the salt revenue of the Yizhou salt lake was effectively a standing military fund, so any armed body that occupied Yizhou struck directly at Jin finances. On the other side stood the village militia raised by Shao Xing on Shenji Mountain northwest of Yizhou. It began with salt workers, farmers, hunters and scattered soldiers from Anyi and Wenxi, mostly migrants who had lost their rations and northern commoners who could not retreat south with the imperial army; numbers grew from a few dozen and a few hundred to several thousand and eventually tens of thousands. The militia had no standing establishment: Shao Xing alone was its chief, with deputy commanders and line leaders taking charge of separate bodies, grain supplied by the stores in the stronghold and by taking it from the enemy, while discipline towards the people was severe — it is recorded that plunder and the taking of captives were forbidden and that soldiers who disturbed the villages were executed, so that the Jin could not make a pretext against them. The Jin treated them as bandits, the local officials treated them as an even greater banditry, and neither side regarded them as an army. At the same time other banners were raised in the north: Cao Cheng’s Eight-Character Army in Shandong, Zhang Rong’s Red Turban Army on Mount Tai, Ma Kuo at Wuma stockade in Hebei. They encouraged one another by answering the call, but there was no unified command and no mechanism for joint action; news passed only sporadically through merchants, mounted couriers and runaway households.
people: Shao Xing was a native of Anyi in Yizhou (in today’s Yuncheng area of Shanxi), born of modest means, famed from his youth for a chivalrous temperament, and his family was well-to-do and given to keeping open house. After Bianjing fell in the second year of Jingkang, he dispersed his wealth, called together the villagers and built a stockade on Shenji Mountain northwest of Yizhou, taking in scattered soldiers of the imperial army and refugees while enrolling the salt workers, woodcutters and hunters around the stockade into his ranks. He knew how to hold a mountain: he cut sheer faces into the rock, blocked the paths and set obstacles, and he used villagers who knew every ravine mouth and salt path as guides, falling back onto the cliffs when the enemy came and striking the rear of the column once the enemy had pushed deep into the defiles. The Jin advanced and were defeated again and again, so they changed to sweeping the hills, cutting the water supply and the grain road, trying to starve the garrison out. The Jin once captured his brother and used him as a hostage to press Shao Xing to surrender; Shao Xing was not moved, refused to trade his brother for his own life, and continued to muster his men and fight as before, and the banners in the mountain were never lowered. The histories say that Shao Xing was skilled at commanding men and could hold his soldiers from molesting the people, which was no easy thing in the disorder of the Jin–Song frontier. On the other side stood the commanders and soldiers mustered by the Jin from Hedong and Henan; the specific names and the numbers of each expedition are glossed over in the chronicles with phrases such as a host or a great army, and the versions differ, so they cannot be checked one by one. The Southern Song court was always in two minds about such northern militias: it wanted to use them to harass the enemy, yet feared they would establish themselves as autonomous powers in the occupied land, so it neither formally incorporated them nor genuinely destroyed them. After the loss of Shaan Prefecture Shao Xing led his people south, withdrew into Shang Prefecture, changed his name to Shao Long, hid between Shang and Luo, took in refugees and taught martial skills for roughly ten years before dying. The main records of his career are found in the Song continuations such as the Jianyan yilai xinian yaolu and the Sanchao Beiming huibian, together with the relevant chapters of the History of Jin; the two sides differ now and then, and details remain contested.

kits: The weapon on the card is the Dane axe, a long-handled axe common in northern Europe between the tenth and twelfth centuries: the haft is longer than a man, the head is narrow and thin, the edge runs from the beard downward and ends in an upturned curl, it is single-edged, and nearly the whole weight of the weapon sits in the head at the front. Swung with both hands on the haft, it gains its power from the curve of the shaft and the mass of the head, and a single blow can split a shield, break a deer-antler palisade or bring down a mounted man. It must be said plainly: this weapon never appeared on the battlefields of Hedong in the Jin–Song war. It belongs to the northern European equipment sequence and is a different technical tradition from the Chinese axe; the card uses it to stand for the essential logic of the form — a narrow head, a single edge, weight traded for destructive force — and the weapon that Shao Xing’s men actually held on Shenji Mountain was the local version of that same logic. His followers were salt workers, farmers and hunters, so what they could buy was chiefly woodcutting axes and heavy axes, together with the padou, the single-edged broad-bladed sword with a slight curve, long-handled sickles, mulberry forks, iron forks and hooked sickles; at range they relied on horn and lacquered bows and the strong crossbow, with stone throwers and sling stones to pin the enemy. Defence rested on cut cliffs, stacked stone, woven bamboo palisades, caltrops, deer-antler obstacles and ditches; at night they fired rockets and fire arrows at the Jin siege towers and baggage carts. The key to holding the Yizhou salt lake was the axe that could cut the roads and the padou that could take a rider’s head, not any single treasured weapon. Viewed as a whole, the armament of this rising was that of a peasant revolt: no state-forged heavy crossbows or siege artillery, no organised baggage train, everything maintained from local materials and from arms taken off the enemy. It is worth noting that the axe lineage was never wholly separate across Eurasia: the Mongol campaigns carried the northern European long-handled axe form into China and carried Chinese axe and sickle workmanship westward, and the comparison of the two forms has never been settled in the history of armaments — the opinions differ.

tactics: At the outset Shao Xing adopted a defensive pattern of holding the mountain and striking when opportunity offered. Shenji Mountain lies northwest of Yizhou town; the heights are not great but run on in a chain of ravines, narrow at the mouths and steep, and therefore easy to defend. The militia cut sheer walls along the ridge, blocked the gorges and set obstacles in the defiles, dug storage caves in the slopes for grain and water, and concentrated the whole supply of the stockade in one place. When the Jin attacked in force, their cavalry could not deploy and no amount of numbers would help them; the militia only had to seal the mouths of the ravines with bows and crossbows, let the enemy press into the narrow track, and then bring down arrows, stones and felled timber on the head and tail of the column. Repeated frontal attacks failed, so the Jin changed to sweeping the hills, cutting the water and the grain road, hoping to force the garrison out. Shao Xing answered a siege with a clearance policy, moving the grain from the villages outside into the mountain first of all, while small bands went out day and night to strike the Jin patrols, salt carts and baggage trains, cutting the salt road and the grain road running from Yizhou to Pingyang and Puzhou. For the Jin the sharpest pain was not the failure to take the stockade but the severed salt revenue; the core of Shao Xing’s method was to occupy the place that produced the money so that the other side could not collect it. The order of battle was rough but effective: bows and crossbows in front, axes and blades behind, infantry in the centre, very few horsemen, ambushes laid in the gorges, hit and withdraw, and never a set-piece array in the open. In morale, the Jin seized Shao Xing’s brother as a pledge and pressed for surrender many times over, and he was not moved; the longer the garrison held out in the mountain, the stronger that constancy became as a call to arms. In the end the Jin applied heavy pressure on the Shaan Prefecture axis: around the first year of Shaoxing (1131) Shaan fell, the door of Hedong was thrown wide, and both Shao Xing’s retreat and his supplies were cut. He then abandoned the stockade, took his lightly equipped columns south by the valleys and small tracks in scattered order to avoid the Jin horse, and reached Shang Prefecture in Shaanxi by a circuitous route, never meeting the Jin in open battle again. As for why the rising finally failed, the answer lies in the method as well: terrain could hold the enemy for years, but there was no sustainable rear, no unified command, and no supply line that could be joined to the regular Southern Song army; after a long war the numbers dispersed and the stockade and the banner could not be held.

data: There are not many figures that can be checked, so only those with a basis are listed. In the first month of the second year of Jingkang (1127) the Jin took Bianjing, the emperors Huizong and Qinzong were carried north, and the Northern Song ended; most prefectures in the north fell away in the same year, and Shao Xing rose not long afterwards in Yizhou. From 1127 until the loss of Shaan Prefecture in 1131 the militia stood against the Jin for some four or five years; the chronicles describe endless engagements, and the Jin mustered several expeditions to suppress it, but the numbers of men in each are given only as a host or a great army, with no verifiable figures, so no headcount is tabulated here. The scale of the militia can likewise only be described in general: it started with salt workers and farmers from Anyi and Wenxi, grew from hundreds to thousands, and was later swelled by refugees and scattered soldiers, while the chronicles speak of tens of thousands — but such numbers were often rhetorical exaggeration at the time and should not be read as real totals. As for distance, Shenji Mountain lies no more than some tens of li from Yizhou town, and the track from the stockade to the salt lake is within a hundred li, so the militia’s control of the lake was a close, constant business rather than a single raid. The importance of the lake can be inferred from the finances: Yizhou was the largest salt-producing district in the Jin north and salt revenue was one of the main sources of income in Hedong, so holding the lake meant intercepting a direct flow of revenue into the treasury, and it was precisely this that drew the larger suppression expeditions. On the far end of the timeline lies the loss of Shaan Prefecture around the first year of Shaoxing (1131): that city was the hinge through which the Jin moved men and grain from Hedong into Guanzhong, and once it fell Shao Xing gave up the stockade, led his people south to Shang Prefecture, changed his name to Shao Long, lived in hiding between Shang and Luo for some ten years, and was dead by the early 1140s at the latest. The other northern militias of the same period — Cao Cheng’s Eight-Character Army, Zhang Rong’s Red Turban Army, Ma Kuo’s Wuma stockade — mostly rose between 1127 and 1131 and were put down in turn; in 1141 the Song–Jin peace conference fixed the frontier, and no more organised Han Chinese forces remained in the north.

cause: The immediate cause of this rising lay in the fall of the capital. In the first month of the second year of Jingkang (1127) the Jin breached Bianjing, carried off the emperors Huizong and Qinzong together with much of the imperial clan and the court, and the Northern Song dissolved in a single night; the governments of the Hedong prefectures immediately lost their superiors, the county troops scattered, and order broke down. Beneath that lay the way the new dynasty ruled: in the early years the Jin reorganised households and land in the north by registering people and fields and taking them into bonds, writing the Han population into a frame of metal control, with a graduated tax system and a hierarchy by ethnicity, and the cry that the foreigners were the enemy became the outlet for popular resentment; among the salt workers and furnace households of Yizhou the burden of the salt levy and of corvée was heaviest, and these were households whose tools — the wood axe and the heavy axe — were already weapons at hand. Third came the vacuum: when the main body of the Jin army withdrew north in 1127, a brief opening of power appeared across Hebei, Shandong and Hedong, soldiers were discharged, disaster refugees moved, temples, merchants and local magnates armed themselves, and a village notable such as Shao Xing had room to make his appeal — preserve the home, keep a living, drive out the Jin. Fourth was the opening: the Jin’s weight shifted to the Huai and Han river lines, the Hedong garrison was comparatively empty, and the militia could stand its ground in the hills and continue for five years by hit-and-run. Fifth was organisation and leadership. Shao Xing came from a comfortable Anyi family, had money, local connections and a network among the salt workers, and could disperse his wealth to gather men, build a stockade and drill soldiers, and in a time of short grain and short arms he could buy support by forbidding his men to molest the people; the histories say he was skilled at commanding men, and that is why the rising lasted instead of dispersing in a single rush. From without there was almost no help: neither Song troops nor Song grain ever reached Hedong in strength, so the militia fought essentially alone — a fact that already foretold the end.

impact: In the short term, the rising pinned down the Jin’s attention in Hedong for four or five years. The court had to detach part of the troops mustered from Henan, Hebei and Shandong to the suppression of Yizhou, and Hedong was one of the corridors along which the Jin moved men and grain toward Guanzhong and Sichuan; for every day the rising held the ground, the corridor grew more risky. The larger significance was the demonstration: around 1127 a number of uprisings rose together in the north — Cao Cheng’s Eight-Character Army, Zhang Rong’s Red Turban Army, Ma Kuo’s Wuma stockade — and Shao Xing was the one who held ground in a producing district, the salt lake, and kept discipline by not molesting the people. He showed those who came later that a mountainous and frontier land could raise a resisting force out of local society itself, without waiting for the imperial army. For the Southern Song these militias were an awkward resource: the court needed them to harry the enemy in the north, yet never dared incorporate them formally, fearing that they would establish themselves in the lost provinces and that there would be no troops to bring the reconquered land under control; their existence therefore remained in the state of answering the call without acting in concert — neither disciplined like regular troops nor supported from the rear — and this structural contradiction had no solution once the peace conference of Shaoxing settled the frontier: with the border drawn, the northern militias lost their reason to exist and were put down or disbanded one by one. In the long run, Han Chinese resistance to the Jin between 1115 and 1234 took two forms: early on, risings of this kind built on local society and unequal in scale; later, harrying warfare carried out by Southern Song units holding mountain fortresses. Shao Xing’s life in Shang Prefecture, taking pupils and teaching martial skills, sits between the two and shows a transitional form in which local military force was preserved. For historians, the Shao Xing rising is a window onto northern society in the early Jin: salt economics, the registration of households and people, village self-defence and ethnic identity can all be traced in a rising of this modest size.

Shao Xing’s life in Shang Prefecture, taking pupils and teaching martial skills, sits between the two and shows a transitional form in which local military force was preserved. For historians, the Shao Xing rising is a window onto northern society in the early Jin: salt economics, the registration of households and people, village self-defence and ethnic identity can all be traced in a rising of this modest size.
result: In military terms the rising did not succeed. After building the stockade on Shenji Mountain, Shao Xing used the terrain and the local men who knew it to defeat several Jin attacks, throwing them into ambushes in the ravines and cutting their supply road; the Jin took his brother as a hostage and pressed for surrender many times, and he was never moved. After a stalemate of some four or five years the situation turned decisively: around the first year of Shaoxing (1131) the Jin took Shaan Prefecture, the gates and key positions of Hedong were lost, and Shao Xing had neither a rear to fall back on nor rations to hold out with; to go on sitting in the mountain would only have been encirclement. He therefore abandoned the stockade he had built over several years, led lightly equipped columns out through the encirclement, went south by the valleys and small tracks in dispersed order to avoid the cavalry, and by a circuitous route reached Shang Prefecture in Shaanxi. With that the stage of northern resistance through armed risings came to an end. In Shang Prefecture he changed his name to Shao Long, hid between Shang and Luo, and for about ten years no longer met the Jin in battle, taking in refugees and teaching martial skills to keep himself alive; he died of illness there, and his men scattered, some returning to the fields, some dispersed with the demobilisation that followed the peace. The northern militias as a whole were extinguished in the same period: Cao Cheng’s Eight-Character Army disintegrated on the Shandong front after its retreat, the forces of Zhang Rong and Ma Kuo were put down in turn, and no organised Han Chinese force remained in the north until the Southern Song adopted the fortress-and-harassment system. For the Jin this was a successful suppression: the salt revenue of Hedong returned to the treasury, the roads through Shaan and Yizhou were open again, rule in Shanxi was consolidated, and the troops could be moved south. For posterity the meaning of the Shao Xing rising lies more in memory and example: a villager of Yizhou, with one mountain, one salt lake and a band of villagers unwilling to surrender, held the Jin for years; he set not molesting the people as his discipline and cutting grain and salt as his method, and although he never held a city, he left in the north a story of resistance against the Jin that is still remembered.
